refined_text:
The FreeRTOS priority inversion incident occurred when the high priority telemetry task blocked on a shared resource held by the low priority logging task. The low priority worker acquired a standard binary semaphore before initiating sensor readings. Before the logger released the semaphore, a medium priority networking worker preempted execution, starving the low priority task for over 50 milliseconds. Because the binary semaphore lacked priority inheritance mechanisms, the critical telemetry worker remained blocked despite having priority 4 instead of priority 2.

Replacing the binary semaphore with a mutex established priority inheritance across shared peripheral drivers. When the telemetry task attempts to acquire the locked mutex, the FreeRTOS scheduler temporarily elevates the low priority logging task priority to match the blocked worker. The logger finishes its memory write operations without further preemption from intermediate tasks. Releasing the mutex restores the original priority level and yields processor execution to the telemetry thread within 20 microseconds.

In direct mode, all asynchronous interrupts and synchronous traps jump to a single base address. By setting the low 2 bits of mtvec to 1 instead of 0, the core switches to vectored mode where each exception cause offsets into an aligned jump table.

When the machine timer interrupt fires with mcause code 7, hardware automatically preserves the program counter in mepc. The trap vector jumps directly to the timer service routine without requiring software dispatch decoding. The service routine programs the next compare threshold in mtimecmp before executing the mret instruction. Executing mret restores the previous execution mode from mstatus and resumes user code at the address stored in mepc.

When the sensor resets mid-transaction, its state machine continues driving the SDA line low, blocking all subsequent bus transfers. Because the hardware TWIM master cannot generate clock pulses while SDA remains asserted, software recovery intervention is necessary before resuming normal communication.

The recovery routine disables the TWIM block and reconfigures SCL and SDA as general purpose GPIO outputs. Manually toggling the SCL line generates 9 clock pulses, allowing the stuck slave to shift out its remaining data bits and release the SDA line. After generating a manual STOP condition, the firmware re-enables the TWIM peripheral with EasyDMA pointers, restoring regular sensor transactions without requiring a full board power cycle.

The RP2040 dual-core firmware crashed with an unpredictable hard fault during flash sector erase operations. While Core 0 executed the internal ROM flash erasing function, Core 1 attempted to fetch application instructions from the external QSPI flash memory. Because the QSPI flash hardware cannot service memory reads while an erase cycle is active, Core 1 read invalid opcode patterns that crashed the processor.

Resolving the flash access conflict required synchronizing both cores via the inter-core FIFO prior to flash writes. Core 0 sends a pause command over the FIFO, forcing Core 1 to park in a tight loop inside internal SRAM. Furthermore, placing the flash erase driver inside 4096 bytes of reserved RAM prevents Core 0 from accessing QSPI during the operation. Once the sector erase finishes, Core 0 signals Core 1 to resume normal execution.

The safety-critical firmware employs the STM32 window watchdog WWDG to detect software execution anomalies and timing deviations. Unlike standard independent watchdogs, the window watchdog requires periodic counter refreshes strictly within an allowed time window. Refreshing the counter too early while its value remains above the window threshold triggers an immediate system reset.

During peripheral initialization, the firmware programs the window threshold to 80 and loads initial counter value 0x7f into the control register. Setting the early warning interrupt EWI bit in the configuration register arms a high-priority interrupt handler. When the downcounter drops to 0x40 without receiving a scheduled refresh, the interrupt routine logs CPU diagnostic registers to flash memory before the hardware triggers an MCU reset.
